weighted_rating: Whenever the votes are a fraction (2.5), they are used as is in the calculation.

gross_receipts: Whenever every counted amount is a whole number, the total is a whole number; whenever any counted amount has decimals the total is a decimal number (100.5 and 200 give 300.5), using ordinary floating point addition (0.1 and 0.2 give 0.30000000000000004).

gross_receipts: Whenever amounts are text, a number in the text is used ('100' and '250.5' give 350.5; '12x' counts as 12; '1e2' counts as 100.0); text with no leading number counts as 0 and adds nothing.
gross_receipts: Whenever it is used with GROUP BY, each group is totalled separately by the same rules (a group with only refunds gives 0), and rows removed by WHERE are not counted.
gross_receipts: Whenever DISTINCT is written inside it, it is ignored and every row is still added (amounts 5, 5, 3 give 13, not 8).

slugify: Whenever a title is given, it returns the text in lower case with every run of characters that are not letters a-z or digits 0-9 (spaces, punctuation, tabs, line breaks, underscores, symbols) replaced by one single dash ('Hello, World!' gives 'hello-world'; 'snake_case' gives 'snake-case').
slugify: Whenever the result would begin or end with a dash (leading or trailing spaces or punctuation, such as '  Hello   World  ' or '--Hello--'), those dashes are removed.

slugify: Whenever the title has accented letters, they are reduced to the plain letter ('Café Crème Brûlée' gives 'cafe-creme-brulee'; 'Ça va' gives 'ca-va'), and full-width letters and digits, ligatures and superscripts are also converted to plain ones ('ﬁne' gives 'fine', 'x²' gives 'x2').

slugify: Whenever a letter has no plain-letter form (ß, Æ, Ø, and all non-Latin scripts such as Japanese, and emoji), it is silently deleted rather than turned into a dash or transliterated ('Straße' gives 'strae'; 'Ærø Øl ß' gives 'r-l'; '日本語 Tokyo' gives 'tokyo').

slugify: Whenever the title has typographic dashes or quotes (en dash, em dash, curly quotes), they are deleted and not turned into a dash, so the words either side are joined ('a–b—c' gives 'abc'). A plain apostrophe is also deleted, not turned into a dash ('dog's' gives 'dogs').
slugify: Whenever the title has no letters or digits at all (empty, spaces only, '!!!', or only non-Latin characters), it returns 'untitled', not NULL and not empty text.
slugify: Whenever the title is NULL, it returns NULL.
slugify: Whenever the input is a number (12345 or 12.5), it is treated as its text and a decimal point becomes a dash ('12-5').

mask_card: Whenever a card number has more than 4 digits, it returns one '*' for every digit except the last 4, followed by those last 4 digits ('4111 1111 1111 1111' gives '************1111'), so the result is as long as the number of digits.

mask_card: Spaces and hyphens in the number stay exactly where they are, and the digits are masked as before, so that only the last four digits are shown and every other digit is replaced with '*' ('4111-1111-1111-1111' gives '****-****-****-1111'). Any other non-digit character, such as dots, slashes, underscores or brackets, makes it return 'INVALID'.
mask_card: Whenever the number has 4 or fewer digits, every digit is masked, with one '*' per digit ('1234' gives '****'; '123' gives '***'; '0000' gives '****'), so the last 4 digits are not shown.
mask_card: Whenever the input has no digits at all (empty text or just letters such as 'abcd'), it returns empty text.
mask_card: Whenever the input is NULL, it returns NULL.

mask_card: Whenever the input has letters or other text mixed with digits, only the digits count, and the last 4 digits found are shown even if they come from other text ('4111 1111 1111 1111 exp 12/26' gives '****************1226'; 'XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-1111' gives '****', because the X's and any existing '*' are dropped and only 4 digits remain).

mask_card: Whenever the input is a plain number rather than text (4111111111111111), it is treated as its digits and masked in the same way; a number with a decimal point such as 41.5 counts its digits and not the point (3 digits give '***').
mask_card: Whenever digits are written in non-Western numerals (such as Arabic-Indic digits), they are counted as digits and the last four are shown as written.

spots.say: Nia's order is placed on Monday 2 November and promised for Friday 6 November: the engine counts 4 working days, because the end date itself is not counted.
A job starting Thursday 24 December and ending Monday 28 December, with Christmas Day in between, counts 2 working days, because public holidays are treated as ordinary working days.
A job that ends on Monday 2 November but started on Friday 6 November, entered the wrong way round, shows minus 4 working days instead of an error.
Nia's delivery date typed as 11/06/2026 instead of year-month-day gives no answer at all, so the working-day count is left blank.
Customer Dana's number typed as 1-415-555-0132 is shown as (415) 555-0132, with the leading 1 dropped.
Dana's seven-digit number with no area code, 555-0132, is passed through exactly as typed, so it is not flagged as incomplete.
Dana's office number written with an extension, 415 555 0132 ext 12, is left untidied exactly as typed, because the extra digits push it past ten.
A number with an impossible area code starting in 0, (015) 555-0132, is accepted and shown unchanged as a valid-looking number.
A London customer's number, +44 20 7946 0958, is returned exactly as typed and not rejected, so non-North-American numbers pass through silently.
Priya's course score of exactly 90 earns an A, so 90 is the lowest score that gets an A.
Tom's score of 89.99 earns a B, not an A, so there is no rounding up to the next grade.
Priya's score of 105 with extra credit still earns an A, so scores above 100 are accepted.
A student whose score was left as blank text gets an F rather than an empty grade.
A mistyped score of minus 5 gets an F instead of being flagged as invalid.
Ravi's 100-rupee invoice (10,000 cents) is paid 31 days late: the late fee comes to 1,550 cents, which is 15.50 rupees, charged at half a percent per day.
Ravi's 100-rupee invoice left unpaid for 400 days is charged a late fee of 20,000 cents, twice the invoice itself, because there is no cap.
A 1-rupee invoice (100 cents) paid one day late is charged 1 cent, because half a cent is rounded up and there is no minimum fee.
Ravi's invoice paid 3 days early is charged a late fee of 0, and early payment earns no credit.
Ravi's invoice paid two and a half days late is charged 125 cents, because part-days are charged pro rata rather than rounded to whole days.
Ana's card 4111 1111 1111 1111 prints on the receipt as 12 stars followed by 1111, with the spaces removed.
A card number mistyped as just 411 is shown as 3 stars, so it is hidden completely and nothing flags it as too short.
A card number with too many digits, 4111-1111-1111-1111-123, is accepted and shown with 15 stars then 1123, and it is not rejected.
If a cashier types letters instead of a card number, the receipt shows an empty string, and no mask appears.
A parcel weighing exactly 1 kilogram to zone 2 costs 800 cents, which is 8.00.
The same parcel at 1 gram over a kilogram to zone 2 costs 1,000 cents, 2.00 more, because every started kilogram is billed in full.
A parcel weighing nothing to zone 1 still costs 300 cents, which is 3.00, because there is a base charge.
A parcel sent to zone 0 gets no price at all, which leaves the shipping charge blank.
A 100-kilogram pallet to zone 3 costs 30,900 cents, which is 309.00, because there is no weight limit or cap.
The title 'Café Münster – 50% Off' becomes the web address cafe-munster-50-off, with accents stripped and the percent sign dropped.
A product called '東京 Tower' becomes just tower in its web address, because the Japanese characters are silently thrown away.
A title made only of punctuation, '!!!', produces an empty web address, which would collide with other such titles.
The title '  Spring   Sale  ' with extra spaces becomes spring-sale, so spaces are tidied into single dashes.
Mei orders 9 items at 10.00 each and pays 9,000 cents, which is 90.00 with no discount.
Mei orders 10 items at 10.00 each and pays 9,000 cents, which is 90.00, so the 10% discount starts at exactly 10 items and she pays the same as for 9.
Mei orders 100 items at 10.00 each and pays 90,000 cents, which is 900.00, so ordering ten times as many items earns no bigger discount than 10%.
Mei orders 10 items at 9.95 each and pays 8,955 cents, which is 89.55 after the 10% discount applies to the whole order.
An order for minus 2 items at 10.00 gets no price, which leaves the total blank rather than a refund.
A cafe with a single 5-star vote gets an adjusted rating of 3.18, because the score is pulled strongly toward 3.
A new cafe with no votes shows an adjusted rating of 3.0, the default middle score.
A cafe averaging 4.5 stars from 1,000 votes shows 4.49, so a large number of votes barely moves the score.
A mistyped average of 9 stars from 10 votes gives an adjusted rating of 6.0, which is above the 5-star maximum, because ratings are not capped.
A cafe with minus 1 votes gets no rating, so the score is left blank.
Four payment rows of 100, 250, a refund of minus 50 and one blank add up to gross receipts of 350, because the refund is ignored instead of being subtracted.

dg_cases.say: Dates that carry a time of day, like a job booked from Friday 30 October at 10:00 to Tuesday 3 November at 9:00, are counted by our build as 2 working days (a second build gave no answer at all).
A date typed as a plain number, like 20261030 to 20261103 for Friday 30 October to Tuesday 3 November, is accepted by our build and counted as 2 working days (a second build gave no answer at all).
A date written without the leading zero, like 1 September to 8 September 2026, gets no answer from our build (a second build counted it as 5 working days).

A customer, Dana, gives her office line 415 555 2671 with extension 12: our build keeps the number exactly as she typed it, extension included (a second build rejected it as unusable and kept nothing).
A florist's customer enters the letters-based number 1 (800) FLOWERS: our build keeps it as typed (a second build rejected it as not a valid number and kept nothing).
A London supplier, Oliver, gives his UK number +44 20 7946 0958: our build keeps it as typed (a second build rejected it because it isn't a North American number and kept nothing).
A customer, Maria, leaves out a digit and types only 9 digits, 415555267: our build keeps the incomplete number as typed (a second build rejected it and kept nothing).
Maya's score box was left blank because her exam hasn't been marked yet: our build prints an F on her report card (a second build prints no grade at all).
Daniel's score is entered as "90%" with a percent sign: our build reads it as 90 and gives him an A (a second build doesn't recognise it and prints no grade).
A teacher mistypes the word "abc" instead of Priya's score: our build fails her with an F on the report card (a second build prints no grade and leaves it unresolved).

An invoice whose amount is unreadable (typed as "abc" instead of a number) is 5 days late: our build charges no late fee, $0.00 (a second build gives no answer at all, so the customer is neither charged nor told the fee is zero).

A customer's card number that is only 4 digits long, such as 1234, appears on the receipt as four stars with nothing visible (a second build printed the full number 1234 unmasked, and the same split applies to any card number of 4 digits or fewer).

A customer's order of 5 items comes in with a garbled, non-numeric item price like "abc": our build charges $0.00 for the order, so the items would go out free (a second build gives no price at all, so the order cannot be priced and gets flagged).

A product with 10 votes has its average rating entered as unreadable text ("abc"): our build still gives it an adjusted score of 1.5 stars, treating the bad rating as zero (a second build shows no score at all).

A customer's payment is entered as the text "1,000.50" (with a thousands comma) alongside a separate 5-rupee payment: our build counts only the 5-rupee payment and reports total receipts of 6 (a second build reported 5).
